## Learning outcomes {.unnumbered #sec-s2-outcomes}

By the end of this session you should be able to:

1. Explain why a static test cannot reveal a timing defect, and why a
   sinusoid can.
2. Fit a sinusoid to sampled data by least squares with the frequency as a
   free parameter, and say why the frequency must be fitted rather than
   assumed.
3. Convert a fit residual into an effective number of bits, and state which
   time base produced it.
4. Measure the cost, in bits, of analysing timestamped samples as though they
   lay on a nominal grid.
5. Separate a noise-limited regime from a jitter-limited one, extract the
   aperture jitter, and locate the crossover.
6. Measure one oscillator against another and report the result in ppm with
   the correct sign.
7. Build an uncertainty budget in which the reference instrument, not the
   device under test, may well be the dominant term.

## Prerequisites {#sec-s2-prerequisites}

- [S1](../S1-daq-static/index.qmd), completed. Its noise floor and static
  ENOB are inputs here, and the low-frequency end of this experiment is a
  check on them.
- A conditioning stage built and characterized — see
  [the conditioning board](../../hardware/conditioning-board.qmd).
- Least squares, and enough trigonometry to be comfortable with
  @eq-s2-model.

## Tier 2 — S1's bench plus a source

The one genuinely expensive item on this site's bill of materials is the
signal generator, and it is shared between benches rather than bought per
bench.
:::

| Item | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Streaming board with `UsbIo` | The instrument under test | mbed boards only; the sweep needs tens of kHz |
| Host computer | Acquisition | Linux recommended |
| Signal generator | The reference source | Its noise and distortion must be below the converter's |
| Conditioning stage | Bipolar to unipolar, with headroom | See [the conditioning board](../../hardware/conditioning-board.qmd) |
| Oscilloscope or DMM | Verifying amplitude and headroom at the pin | — |

## Data recording {#sec-s2-recording}

One CSV and one sidecar per sweep point, in the format specified in
[Data format](../../data-format/index.qmd). The checklist in
@sec-s2-step-sidecar is the version to work through at the bench.

What distinguishes an S2 sidecar from an S1 one is `references[]`: the
generator is an instrument used to make the measurement, so its settings and
their uncertainties go there, one entry per quantity.

```{.yaml filename="data/sweep-1000hz.yaml"}
experiment: S2
run: sweep-1000hz
date: 2026-09-18
operator: "your name"
synthetic: false

board:
  model: portenta-h7
  adc_bits: 16
  vref_mV: 3300
  usbio_version: "from arduino-io info"

acquisition:
  pins: [15]
  requested_period_us: 50
  achieved_rate_hz: 0.0        # from the stream summary, not the request
  duration_s: 0.1

stream_stats:                   # all six, from the summary line
  records: 0
  device_overruns: 0
  seq_gaps: 0
  host_drops: 0
  resyncs: 0
  stale_records: 0

channels:
  - pin: 15
    quantity: voltage
    unit: V
    sensor: "sine from bench signal generator, through conditioning board"
    conditioning: {gain: 1.0, offset: 1.65, filter: none}

references:
  - instrument: signal generator
    model: "the model you used"
    calibration: "certificate or none"
    quantity: frequency
    unit: Hz
    reference_value: 998.502    # the exact setting, not the nominal label
    reference_u: 0.005          # from the generator's specification
  - instrument: signal generator
    model: "the model you used"
    calibration: "certificate or none"
    quantity: amplitude
    unit: V
    reference_value: 1.485
    reference_u: 0.0074
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Record the exact frequency, not the label

`sweep-1000hz` is a file name. The frequency that enters @eq-s2-ppm is the
one the generator was actually set to, computed from @eq-s2-coherent with the
**achieved** sampling rate. Writing 1000 in the sidecar when the generator was
set to 998.502 Hz puts a 1500 ppm error into a measurement whose whole purpose
is to resolve tens of ppm.
:::

## Analysis tasks {#sec-s2-tasks}

Open one of the two templates — [Python](analysis-py.qmd) or
[R](analysis-r.qmd) — point it at your files, and work through it. They
contain the same sections and produce the same numbers.

1. **Data quality.** Validate every sidecar and read the stream counters.
2. **One fit, in detail.** Take the middle frequency, fit @eq-s2-model with
   $f$ free, and plot the residual against time. Confirm there is no
   structure in it — no flat tops, no slow trend, no visible harmonic.
3. **ENOB in both time bases.** Repeat the fit on the nominal grid and on
   `t_us`, and report @eq-s2-penalty for every sweep point.
4. **The roll-off.** Plot ENOB against frequency. Compare the low-frequency
   value with S1's static ENOB; they should agree to a few tenths of a bit,
   and the dynamic one can never be the larger.
5. **The jitter limit.** Overlay @eq-s2-jitter-enob, fit $\sigma_j$ to the
   high-frequency end, and find the crossover with S1's noise floor.
6. **Clock accuracy.** Report @eq-s2-ppm for every point, with its sign
   explained, and check that it does not depend on frequency.
7. **Budget.** Build the budget of @sec-s2-budget.

## Uncertainty budget {#sec-s2-budget}

{{< include ../../shared/_uncertainty-budget.qmd >}}

**The measurand** is the device's clock error in ppm, @eq-s2-ppm, evaluated at
the sweep point with the best signal-to-noise ratio. It is chosen over the
amplitude because it is the result a user of this platform actually needs —
every frequency the board ever reports is scaled by it — and because it makes
the experiment's most important lesson arithmetic: the reference instrument,
not the device under test, dominates.

Writing $\delta = 10^6\,(\hat f/f_\mathrm{gen} - 1)$, the sensitivity
coefficients are

$$
\frac{\partial \delta}{\partial \hat{f}} = \frac{10^6}{f_\mathrm{gen}},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \delta}{\partial f_\mathrm{gen}}
  = -\frac{10^6\,\hat{f}}{f_\mathrm{gen}^{2}}
  \approx -\frac{10^6}{f_\mathrm{gen}}
$$ {#eq-s2-ppm-sensitivity}

| Component | Type | Distribution | Source | $c_i$ |
|---|:--:|---|---|---|
| Fitted frequency $\hat f$ | A | — | Standard error of $f$ from the four-parameter fit | $10^6/f_\mathrm{gen}$ |
| Generator frequency | B | — | `reference_u` in the sidecar, from the instrument's specification | $-10^6/f_\mathrm{gen}$ |
| Timestamp quantization | B | Rectangular | One microsecond over the record length, as a bound | $10^6/f_\mathrm{gen}$ |
| Instability across the sweep | B | Rectangular | The spread of $\delta$ over the sweep points — it should not depend on frequency, so whatever spread there is bounds the drift | $10^6/f_\mathrm{gen}$ |

: Components of the S2 budget {#tbl-s2-components}

Report $u_c$ and $U = 2u_c$, the index $h_i$ of every component, and one
sentence naming the dominant term.

::: {.callout-important}
## What this budget is designed to show

On a well-fitted record of a few thousand samples the Type A term is tiny —
the fit locates the frequency to a small fraction of a bin. The generator's
own specification is then almost certainly the largest component, and the
honest conclusion is that **this measurement is limited by the reference, not
by the board**. That is not a failure of the experiment; it is the experiment
working. The way to improve it is a better generator or a longer record, not
a better board, and being able to say which is the point of building a budget
at all.
:::

## Questions {#sec-s2-questions}

1. Why can a static test not detect aperture jitter, however many samples you
   average?
2. The fit estimates four parameters from a few thousand samples. What
   happens to the ENOB if you fix $f$ at the nominal value instead, and why
   does the effect get *worse* with a longer record?
3. Your dynamic ENOB at 10 Hz exceeds your static ENOB from S1 by half a bit.
   What went wrong?
4. Two boards have the same aperture jitter but 12 and 16 nominal bits. At
   what frequency do they become indistinguishable, and what does that say
   about buying resolution?
5. The timing penalty at your highest frequency is several bits. Restate that
   as a statement about a data acquisition system that reports samples without
   timestamps.
6. Your clock accuracy comes out at $-18$ ppm with a generator specified to
   $\pm 5$ ppm. What can you legitimately conclude about the board's
   oscillator?
7. You need 12 effective bits at 5 kHz. Using your own $\sigma_j$, is that
   achievable on this platform? If not, what would have to change?
